deep.reconstruction:
Context: on p.27 Hilbert begins: 'Proof that the Galois field formed from all conjugate fields of an equation with symmetric group ...'. This page continues it.

CLAIM. Let f(x) be of degree n over Q (or a base field k) with Galois group S_n, and let K = k(x_1,...,x_n) be its splitting field. Then K contains no roots of unity except possibly i (besides ±1).

ARGUMENT (modern notation).
(1) Suppose ζ in K is a root of unity, ζ^m = 1, with ζ not in k. ζ is a rational function θ(x_1,...,x_n) of the roots, and θ^m is rational, hence symmetric. So it suffices to find every rational function θ of the roots some power of which is symmetric.
(2) Assertion: θ can only be the alternant Δ = ∏_{i<j}(x_i − x_j), up to a symmetric factor, and the power needed is 2.
(3) Proof sketch. Call the roots α, β, γ, .... θ^m is unchanged by the transposition τ = (α β). So τ(θ) = cθ with c^m = 1. Hilbert asserts that c 'may only differ by a rational factor', i.e. c ∈ k. Since τ² = 1 we get c² = 1, so c = ±1. If c = −1, θ vanishes when α = β, so (α − β) divides θ. 'And so forth' (my completion): the same holds for every transposition. Hence either θ is symmetric, or θ = Δ·S with S symmetric. Then θ² is symmetric, and θ ∈ k(√D) with D = Δ² the discriminant.
(4) Implicit conclusion (mine): ζ lies in the quadratic field k(√D). Over Q the only extra roots of unity a quadratic field can carry are those of Q(i) and of Q(√−3). Hilbert names only i.

GEOMETRY PROGRAMME. Geometry is to be conceived essentially as in Klein's lithographed lectures 'Höhere Geometrie II' (Göttingen 1892/93). After laying the foundations (non-Euclidean geometry), one should:
- ascend, following Lie, to the most general analytic point transformation (group);
- then descend, by adjoining invariant structures, down to Euclidean geometry.
This continues on the next page, where early introduction of imaginary elements is said to be necessary. It is the Erlangen-programme picture of a hierarchy of geometries via subgroups and stabilisers of invariant configurations.
errors: The conclusion 'no roots of unity except possibly i' is incomplete. The quadratic subfield Q(√D) can also be Q(√−3), which contains the primitive cube and sixth roots of unity. Counterexample: x^3 − 2 has Galois group S_3, discriminant −108 = −3·6², and its splitting field contains ω = (−1+√−3)/2.

Unjustified step: the claim that τ(θ)/θ must be a rational (base-field) factor is not proved. A priori it is only an m-th root of unity, possibly itself in K, which is what one wants to exclude. Example: for θ = ζ, τ(ζ) = ζ^a. A sound argument uses that k(ζ)/k is abelian. Its fixed group is a normal subgroup of S_n with abelian quotient, hence contains A_n (n ≥ 2). So k(ζ) ⊆ k(√D).

'und so fort' hides the extension from one transposition to all of them, and the case of mixed sign behaviour. This is easily filled: the transpositions are all conjugate, and divisibility by every x_i − x_j gives divisibility by Δ.

results.what: The splitting field of an S_n-equation has as its only abelian subextension the quadratic field k(√D), so its roots of unity lie in k(√D)
results.modern_name: Maximal abelian subextension of an S_n-extension is k(√disc), since the commutator subgroup [S_n,S_n] = A_n
results.usually_credited_to: Standard consequence of Galois theory (Galois, Jordan; Lagrange/Cauchy on alternating functions); textbook (Weber, Lehrbuch der Algebra)

results.what: A rational function of the roots that changes by a factor under every transposition is the alternant times a symmetric function
results.modern_name: Characterisation of alternating functions / sign character of S_n; Vandermonde determinant

results.what: Programme: geometry via Klein's lectures; ascend to Lie's general point-transformation group, descend by adjoining invariant structures to Euclidean geometry
results.modern_name: Erlangen programme / Klein–Lie hierarchy of transformation groups
results.usually_credited_to: Klein (1872, Erlangen; Höhere Geometrie lectures 1892/93), Lie

deep.surprise_reason: This is a research-notebook remark containing a routine Galois-theoretic fact. The proof is sketchy and slightly incomplete: it misses Q(√−3) and the rationality of the factor is unjustified. The geometry passage is an explicit endorsement of Klein's and Lie's standpoint. Nothing here goes beyond what was standard around 1890–1900.

checkable.asserts: The discriminant of x^3−2 is −3·36, so Q(√D) = Q(√−3) for this S_3 equation.
ω = (−1+√−3)/2 is a primitive cube root of unity lying in Q(√−3) ⊂ splitting field of x^3−2. This is a counterexample to 'only i'.
The alternant changes sign under the transposition of two roots.
The square of the alternant (the discriminant) is invariant, i.e. the power 2 is symmetric.
Discriminant −23: an S_3 cubic whose quadratic resolvent field Q(√−23) contains no roots of unity other than ±1.

transcription_corrections: 'und sofort' should be read as 'und so fort' (= 'and so on'); it is written run together in the manuscript.
Line 5: 'rationale' is an interlinear insertion above 'eine', with a closing bracket after 'eine'. Reading: 'es eine rationale Function der Wurzeln'.
'ist' before 'wird' is struck through in the manuscript; the transcription's handling is correct.
'mit' is inserted above, after 'Wurzeln'; the roots are written as α β γ.
